title: Q&A: What is in China’s new five-year plan for climate change? - Carbon Brief
gist: China's 15th five-year plan for climate change (2026-2030), issued by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment with 18 other departments, adds no major new targets but consolidates existing ones into the first comprehensive climate target system at five-year-plan level. The real signal is directional: a 17% carbon-intensity cut, a 30MtCO2e non-CO2 abatement goal leaning on coal-mine methane and a first-time focus on SF6, plus an explicit push to expand Chinese influence over global climate governance and carbon-market rule-setting under Article 6.

insights.claim: China's 15th five-year plan for a national response to climate change (2026-2030) contains no major new targets and instead consolidates and reaffirms policies already set out in other plans.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Anyone positioned for a Chinese ambition step-up in this document should reset expectations — the incremental policy delta is near zero, so the tradeable signal is in implementation and governance, not headline numbers.
insights.quote: The new plan does not include any major new targets, instead consolidating and reaffirming existing policies.
insights.locator: China has pledged to peak its emissions before 2030

insights.claim: The Chinese climate plan was released in late July by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment jointly with 18 other government departments, including the National Development and Reform Commission and the National Energy Administration.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Co-signature by the top economic planner and the energy regulator means climate targets now carry cross-ministry enforcement weight rather than sitting in an environmental silo — raising the odds of follow-through in industrial and power policy.
insights.locator: The Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE) released the plan in late July

insights.claim: For the first time at five-year-plan level, China has created a comprehensive target system covering all areas of climate policy, which officials describe as the main policy instrument for climate action during 2026-2030.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A single consolidated target architecture makes Chinese climate policy easier to track and benchmark — future slippage becomes visible against one document rather than scattered across a dozen plans.
insights.locator: For the first time at the five-year plan level

insights.claim: China rarely issues high-level multi-year policies dedicated specifically to responding to climate change; the previous comparable document was an NDRC plan published in 2014 running to 2020 that was not tied to a five-year-plan cycle.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The rarity is the point — binding climate policy to the five-year-plan cycle institutionalises it inside the core planning apparatus, making it harder to deprioritise during growth scares.
insights.locator: China rarely issues high-level multi-year policies

insights.claim: ClearBlue Markets principal analyst Qin Yan argues the plan shows Chinese climate governance has reached an unprecedented strategic level and creates an all-encompassing target system supporting the country's 2030 and 2035 Paris Agreement pledges.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Market-side analysts reading elevated strategic status into the document supports a higher long-run floor on Chinese carbon-price and compliance-demand expectations.
insights.locator: Qin Yan, principal analyst at ClearBlue Markets

insights.claim: CIB Research, an economic research body affiliated with Industrial Bank whose largest shareholder is the Fujian provincial government, frames the plan as marking a new phase focused on strengthening China's climate-governance system, implementation mechanisms and underlying capacity.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: State-linked financial research treating this as a governance-capacity build signals that Chinese banks expect climate compliance to become an operational cost line for industrials, not a soft aspiration.
insights.locator: The five-year plan marks a new phase in China’s climate policy

insights.claim: China's plan reiterates a target of cutting carbon intensity by 17% across the 2026-2030 five-year period.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A 17% intensity cut over five years is a growth-adjusted constraint, not an absolute cap — Chinese emissions can still rise if GDP outruns it, which matters for global coal and gas demand modelling.
insights.quote: Cutting carbon intensity by 17% across the five years
insights.locator: These include:

insights.claim: Industries covered by China's national carbon market face a target of reducing carbon intensity per product by 3% over the plan period.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A product-level intensity benchmark inside the ETS defines the tightening path for covered sectors and sets the baseline against which allowance scarcity — and price — will be calibrated.
insights.quote: Reducing carbon intensity per product in industries under China’s carbon market by 3%
insights.locator: These include:

insights.claim: China's standing pledges are to peak emissions before 2030 with carbon intensity more than 65% below 2005 levels, and — per Xi Jinping's 2035 pledge announced last year — to cut greenhouse gas emissions to 7-10% below peak levels by 2035 while striving to do better.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A 7-10% cut from peak by 2035 is a shallow decline curve; it implies Chinese fossil demand plateaus rather than collapses this decade, which is bullish for the duration of coal and oil cashflows versus aggressive-transition scenarios.
insights.locator: In its 2030 pledge, China aimed to peak emissions

insights.claim: The plan restates support for the 'free flow' of cleantech alongside fossil-fuel-to-renewables substitution and strengthened climate adaptation.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Language on free flow of cleantech is a trade-policy marker aimed at export barriers on Chinese solar, battery and EV supply — watch it resurface in tariff and WTO disputes.
insights.locator: These include:

insights.claim: China reaffirms a target of building non-CO2 greenhouse gas emissions 'reduction capacity' totalling 30m tonnes of CO2 equivalent by 2030, though the baseline for the figure is unclear.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: An unclear baseline makes the headline number hard to verify — treat 30MtCO2e as a directional signal for methane-abatement project demand rather than a measurable emissions outcome.
insights.locator: This includes reaffirming a target of an emissions

insights.claim: iGDP's Chen Meian judges the 30MtCO2e non-CO2 goal 'relatively achievable', noting that ventilation air methane and coal-mine methane projects with concentrations below 8% could alone deliver around 20MtCO2e of reduction by 2030 versus roughly 4.5MtCO2e of annual reductions such projects generate today.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A roughly fourfold expansion of coal-mine methane abatement implies a sizeable build-out of ventilation-air-methane capture equipment and a pipeline of CCER credit supply — a directly investable niche.
insights.quote: generate annual emission reductions of approximately 4.5MtCO2e
insights.locator: The goal refers to emissions reductions

insights.claim: Chen Meian expects measures targeting industrial nitrous oxide and hydrofluorocarbons to make up the remainder of the non-CO2 target beyond coal-mine methane.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: N2O catalyst retrofits and HFC destruction are cheap per tonne abated — chemical producers exposed to adipic/nitric acid and refrigerant lines face compliance capex but also credit-generation upside.
insights.locator: In addition, Chen says, measures targeting industrial nitrous oxide

insights.claim: iGDP analysis of China's UNFCCC biennial reports puts 2021 Chinese greenhouse gas emissions at around 14,000MtCO2e excluding land use, of which non-CO2 gases accounted for roughly 2,700MtCO2e, or 19%, mostly methane.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: The 30MtCO2e abatement goal is roughly 1% of China's ~2,700MtCO2e non-CO2 footprint — a useful reality check on how marginal the target is against the underlying stock of super-pollutant emissions.
insights.locator: According to iGDP analysis of biennial reports

insights.claim: The plan calls for recovery and replacement of sulphur hexafluoride in power equipment, which Chen Meian flags as the standout element because the gas is finally receiving policy attention ahead of Chinese power-system expansion.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: SF6 rules create a replacement cycle in switchgear and grid equipment — watch manufacturers of SF6-free high-voltage gear as grid capex scales in China.
insights.locator: For Chen, the plan’s focus on SF6 control

insights.claim: China's plan sets an explicit 2030 objective of markedly increasing its 'influence, guiding power, shaping power and moral appeal' in global climate governance and building a new narrative on climate governance.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Codifying soft-power objectives in a domestic planning document means climate diplomacy becomes a measured deliverable for Chinese officials — expect more assertive Chinese positions at COP and in standards bodies.
insights.quote: influence, guiding power, shaping power and moral appeal
insights.locator: By 2030, it says China should markedly increase

insights.claim: The plan links China's climate action to the Global Governance Initiative, a policy initiative aimed at reforming the global governance system.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: Climate is being folded into China's broader institutional-reform agenda, meaning climate cooperation may become a bargaining chip in wider geopolitical negotiations rather than a standalone track.
insights.quote: build a new narrative on climate governance
insights.locator: It says China’s climate action could also feed into

insights.claim: Oxford Blavatnik School professor Thomas Hale reads the plan as marking a major rhetorical shift towards China being increasingly willing to lead and shape global climate action.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: If China moves from rule-taker to rule-shaper, Western-designed carbon standards and border adjustments face a competing centre of gravity — a medium-term risk to the assumption that EU rules set the global template.
insights.locator: Prof Thomas Hale, a professor in public policy

insights.claim: The plan directs China to expand the global influence of its carbon market through international rule-setting, cooperation on standards and by hosting the China Carbon Market Conference.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: China is treating carbon-market design as an export product; standards convergence or divergence with the EU ETS will drive cross-border credit fungibility and pricing.
insights.locator: The plan calls for China to expand the global influence

insights.claim: Qin Yan points to the launch of an open coalition on compliance carbon markets with the EU and Brazil as evidence China's more active global carbon-pricing role is already underway, with a work plan expected to be adopted at the China Carbon Market Conference in September.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A dated catalyst — the September conference work plan is a concrete near-term event for carbon-market watchers to position around.
insights.locator: Qin says China’s more active role in global carbon pricing

insights.claim: Qin Yan argues China could become the world's largest buyer of carbon offsets as its energy transition progresses, giving it a direct interest in shaping global rules under the Paris Agreement's Article 6 framework.
insights.speaker: Carbon Brief Staff
insights.so_what: A Chinese pivot to net offset buyer would transform Article 6 demand and credit pricing — the single most consequential non-obvious call in the piece for carbon-credit developers and registries.
insights.quote: could become the world’s largest [carbon] offset buyer
